417.t: Making Breezin': This Masquerade in one take, and Bobby Womack
417.s: An engineer adjusts the vocal EQ, This Masquerade is done in one take, and Bobby Womack supplies the lick that defines Breezin'.
417.q: nothing, no edges. Most of the things we did were first takes. This Masquerade was only one take. Everything went so – everybody was so happy. I was so happy with what I was hearing back from the engineer. The thing that I had with him, I didn’t have with Creed Taylor. I couldn’t make any comments…

417.t: Breezin' origins with Gabor Szabo; orchestra overdubs and the $45,000 cost
417.s: He explains Gabor Szabo's simple tune, LiPuma's playing the record at Warner Bros., the Claus Ogerman string sessions, and how cheaply it was made.
417.q: But Gabor did not think the song was going to be anything. So he took his name off of it. He didn’t care whether his name got on there. He didn’t care. He thought it was going to be nothing, because it was so simple. It was just, do-re-mi-fa-sol-la-ti-do. And it was a – they threw it together at…

417.t: Weekend in L.A.: finding the tempo of On Broadway
417.s: At the Roxy he started On Broadway too slowly, and corrected the tempo in the second set.
417.q: Weekend in L.A., live. That’s where I told the story about my grandfather and my father meeting up for the first time in 21 years and, for me, 31 years. That was an exciting day. One quirk we had. On the first night, when we recorded On Broadway, I didn’t quite know where the tempo should be. So I…

417.t: Donny Hathaway and recording The World Is a Ghetto with Harvey Mason
417.s: Benson recalls hanging out and writing with Donny Hathaway, then cutting The World Is a Ghetto in one take with Harvey Mason.
417.q: Yeah. There were two incredible singers out at the time, Donny Hathaway and Stevie Wonder. They both were just dynamic. I hung out for a short while with Donny Hathaway. I actually wrote a song with him which I found out later he recorded. But just to hang out in his company, I felt big-time. Say,…

417.t: Working with Quincy Jones: 'go for the throat'
417.s: After meeting Quincy at a party and a big band show, Benson chooses to go for a hit and Quincy assembles an A team including drummer John Robinson.
417.q: Have to go back to the beginning of that. I had been bumping into Quincy Jones in various places in the USA. I remember one time, in Chicago, we were at the Hancock building at some party or something. It was the first time that we got an inkling that we might work together. I said, “Man, I’m…

417.t: Give Me the Night: Ivan Lins songs, Bruce Swedien, Rod Temperton's lyrics
417.s: Quincy plays him world music, they pick Ivan Lins tunes, record for a month with Swedien, and Rod Temperton writes many sets of lyrics.
417.q: records from all over the world. He played me African records. He played me Latino records. Then he played stuff from Brazil. Then we heard this song. [Benson scat sings Ivan Lins’s melody Love Dance.]. I said, “What in the world is that? That’s mean.” We put it on. Then he played another song…

417.t: Give Me the Night: the last tune, the B-side trick and Quincy's persuasion
417.s: The final song is recorded with Lee Ritenour using a raspy vocal; Quincy puts the instrumental on the B side and convinces executives to release the title song first.
417.q: But it didn’t get into the album. But what he replaced it with was – I can’t cry. The album sold five million copies. After we finished the whole record, he calls me up. “We got one more tune.” I said, “No, Q, come on.” He said, “No, George, I’m telling you. Rod wrote this one – it’s one more tune.…

746.t: Duo recording with Georg Graewe on detuned pianos
746.s: A piano factory tuner offered unusual tunings for her duo album with Graewe, which sounds like music from outer space.
746.q: Well that was with this German pianist Georg Graewe and we just had the idea to do a duo recording. We went to this piano factory to look at pianos and the master tuner there said he was working with all these different tunings and would we like to try something with one of those tunings, and we…

59.t: Records for MGM with the harpsichord piano sound
59.s: An MGM contract came from imitating a French-popular harpsichord-piano sound, after which he played better material.
59.q: MGM was a company that I’ve recorded for that wanted me to play like a particular recording that was beginning to be popular in France I remember. And it involved a harpsichord piano, that is a grand piano with staples in the hammers so it gave it a clangy sound. It’s useful actually for a…

526.t: Dinner Music with Stuff and Richard Tee
526.s: Her Dinner Music session used overdubs with the band Stuff, where Richard Tee took over the rhythm section and 'Song Sung Long' is discussed.
526.q: It was the rhythm section. And actually, you know it was Richard Tee that just took the session over. Even though it was my record, he just said, “ok now,” and he would tell everybody what they’re gonna do. “You’re gonna play on the second chorus, and over here Eric’s gonna play that thing over…

589.t: Recording Sun Goddess with Earth, Wind and Fire
589.s: Maurice White brings members to Chicago to record Hot Dog It and Sun Goddess; the album outsells the single.
589.q: I’m recording this album in Chicago, and I knew that we had to stop for a couple days, because I had a concert to play in Washington, D.C. So we did. We went and played this concert. 227.ch: Sinatra, Shirley Horn and film songs
227.q: He said, “Can you make the records that bad?” I said, “Don’t worry, we can make them rotten.”

528.s: Tyner says he wanted a contrasting sound on Trident and wanted to avoid repeating a project.
